To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combined effects of prednisolene and cyclosporine on pancreatic B cells of rats during short-term treatment are protective, and that prednisolone might be useful for the prophylaxis of cyclosporine-induced diabetes mellitus.

the combined effects of prednisolones and cyclosporins on the function and morphological changes of pancreatic B cells were studied in Wistar rats and the results showed that prednisolone did not aggravate the damage of pancreatic B cell induced by cyclosporin during short term treatment.

the combined effects of cyclosprin (CYA; 20 mg/kg/d, po) and prednisone (PSL; 3 mg/kg/d, i.m.) on the function and morpholgy of pancreatic B cells were investigated in rats; glucose tolerance was equally impaired by the two treatments, and the pancreatic insulin content in rats treated with CYA alone was 49.8% of that in control animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of prednisone (a synthetic glucocorticoid) on cyclosporine (a calcineurin inhibitor)-induced damage of pancreatic B-cells in Wistar rats.
the effects of CYA and PSL on pancreatic B cell morphology and function in rats.

the effects of PSL and CYA on pancreatic islet B cell function and morphology, and the results suggest that PSL might be protective against the toxic effects of short-term treatment with CYA on B cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PSL is not a risk factor in terms of the development of diabetes during short-term treatment with CYA.
PSL has no deleterious effects, and may be protective, on the pancreatic beta cell during short-term treatment with CYA.
CYA-induced pancreatic B cell injury was not exacerbated by PSL treatment in the present study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of CYA and PSL is not as deleterious to B cells as is the administration of CYA alone.
PSL might protect the pancreatic B cells during CYA therapy, but this protection may be lost with long-term therapy.
PSL is a useful adjuvant in the treatment of diabetes mellitus with CYA, although the mechanism of this effect is unknown.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prednisolone does not exacerbate the toxic effects on pancreatic beta cells of cyclosporine during short-term treatment.
PSL might be protective against cyclosporin A (CsA) damage of pancreatic B cell during the short term.
the combination of PSL and CYA is not associated with an increased incidence of new-onset diabetes mellitus.
